```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor":"#F1F5F9","axes.facecolor":"#F1F5F9",
    "axes.spines.top":False,"axes.spines.right":False,
    "axes.edgecolor":"#CBD5E1","axes.labelcolor":"#334155",
    "axes.labelsize":12,"xtick.labelsize":10,"ytick.labelsize":10,
    "xtick.color":"#94A3B8","ytick.color":"#94A3B8",
    "lines.linewidth":2.2,"font.family":"DejaVu Sans",
    "grid.color":"#E2E8F0","grid.linewidth":0.7,
    "legend.fontsize":10,"legend.framealpha":0.92,
    "legend.edgecolor":"#E2E8F0","figure.dpi":130,
})

TEAL="#0D9488"; ORANGE="#F97316"; GREEN="#22C55E"
NAVY="#1A3A5C"; RED="#EF4444"; GRAY="#94A3B8"

# ── Dataset ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
np.random.seed(42)
dates = pd.date_range(start="2018-01-01", end="2022-12-31", freq="B")
returns = []
for d in dates:
    if   d < pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01"):  returns.append(np.random.normal( 0.0004, 0.008))
    elif d <= pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"): returns.append(np.random.normal(-0.0008, 0.035))
    else:                                  returns.append(np.random.normal( 0.0005, 0.014))

df = pd.DataFrame({"Date": dates, "Return": returns})
df["Price"]    = 100 * (1 + df["Return"]).cumprod()
df["Trend"]    = df["Price"].rolling(90, center=True).mean()
df["RolVol"]   = df["Return"].rolling(30).std()
df["Period"]   = np.where(df["Date"] < "2020-03-01", "Pre-COVID",
                 np.where(df["Date"] <= "2020-06-30", "COVID Shock", "Post-Shock"))

SHOCK = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01")
mean_r = df["Return"].mean(); std_r = df["Return"].std()
df["Anomaly"] = abs(df["Return"] - mean_r) > 3 * std_r
anomalies = df[df["Anomaly"]]
```

     SLIDE 2 — WHAT IS A TIME SERIES?
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## What Is a Time Series?

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

A **time series** is simply a list of measurements collected one after another over time.

What makes it special — the **order of rows matters.** Monday connects to Tuesday. You cannot shuffle the data like a survey without losing information.

**Two ingredients every time series needs:**

<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:10px; margin-top:12px;">
<div class="card card-teal" style="padding:12px 14px;">
  <div style="font-size:1.4em; margin-bottom:4px;">📅</div>
  <strong>Timestamp</strong><br>
  <span style="font-size:0.85em; color:var(--dgray);">When was it measured? (date, hour…)</span>
</div>
<div class="card card-orange" style="padding:12px 14px;">
  <div style="font-size:1.4em; margin-bottom:4px;">📏</div>
  <strong>Value</strong><br>
  <span style="font-size:0.85em; color:var(--dgray);">What was recorded at that time?</span>
</div>
</div>

::: {.info}
💡 **Our example:** Stock market daily returns, 2018–2022. The COVID shock creates a clear "before and after" — perfect for learning every concept.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.13)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.0)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--")

ax.annotate("① Calm — small\nregular changes",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2019-01-01"), 116),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2018-03-01"), 128),
            fontsize=9.5, color=TEAL, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=TEAL, lw=1.3))
ax.annotate("② COVID Shock\n— huge drop",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2020-04-10"), 88),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2020-05-20"), 74),
            fontsize=9.5, color=ORANGE, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ORANGE, lw=1.3))
ax.annotate("③ Recovery\n— bouncing back",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2021-07-01"), 152),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2021-09-01"), 130),
            fontsize=9.5, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREEN, lw=1.3))

ax.set_xlabel("Date"); ax.set_ylabel("Market Index (starts at 100)")
ax.set_title("Stock Market Index — a classic time series", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

     SLIDE 3 — TREND + VOLATILITY
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Two Key Concepts: Trend & Volatility

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
### 📈 Trend — the Big-Picture Direction

The trend is the **overall direction** of the series — ignoring the day-to-day noise. Found by taking a rolling mean (average of the last N days).

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=TEAL, linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.28, label="Daily (noisy)")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Trend"], color=NAVY, linewidth=2.6, label="90-day trend line")
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--", label="COVID shock")
ax.set_ylabel("Index Value"); ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
The navy line removes the noise — now the **up → crash → recover** story is obvious.
:::
:::

::: {}
### 📊 Volatility — How Wild Is It?

Volatility = **standard deviation** of daily changes. High volatility means the series is jumping around a lot. Low = calm and predictable.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, color=RED, linewidth=2.2, label="30-day rolling volatility")
ax.fill_between(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, alpha=0.12, color=RED)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")

pv  = (df["RolVol"]*100).max()
pdt = df.loc[(df["RolVol"]*100).idxmax(),"Date"]
ax.annotate(f"Peak ≈ {pv:.1f}%\n(4× normal)",
            xy=(pdt, pv), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), pv*0.82),
            fontsize=9.5, color=RED, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=RED, lw=1.4))
ax.set_ylabel("Volatility (% / day)"); ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
⚡ COVID made the market **4× more volatile** — risk jumped overnight.
:::
:::
:::

---

<!-- ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE 4 — STATIONARITY + STRUCTURAL BREAK
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Two More Concepts: Stationarity & Structural Break

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
### 🔄 Stationarity — Does It Stay Consistent?

A series is **stationary** when its average and spread stay roughly the same over time. Most analysis tools need this.

The raw price keeps rising forever → **not stationary.**
The daily % change bounces around zero → **stationary.**

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 3.4), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=RED, linewidth=1.5)
axes[0].set_title("❌ Price level — drifts, not stationary", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Index"); axes[0].grid(axis="y")

axes[1].plot(df["Date"], df["Return"]*100, color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.85)
axes[1].axhline(0, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--")
axes[1].set_title("✅ Daily % change — bounces around zero, stationary", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=TEAL)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Change (%)"); axes[1].set_xlabel("Date"); axes[1].grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {}
### 💥 Structural Break — When Everything Changes

A structural break is a point where the series **permanently changes its behaviour.** Models trained before the break will fail after it.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, color=RED, linewidth=2.0)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.2, linestyle="--", label="Break point")

pre_m  = df[df["Date"] < SHOCK]["RolVol"].mean() * 100
post_m = df[df["Date"] > pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30")]["RolVol"].mean() * 100
ax.axhline(pre_m,  xmax=0.47, color=TEAL,  linewidth=2.4, label=f"Before avg: {pre_m:.2f}%")
ax.axhline(post_m, xmin=0.53, color=GREEN, linewidth=2.4, label=f"After avg: {post_m:.2f}%")

ax.set_ylabel("30-day Volatility (%)"); ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.set_title("Spread nearly doubled — and stayed there", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.dark}
Volatility before COVID: **~0.8%/day.** After COVID: **~1.4%/day.** Old models stopped working. This is a structural break.
:::
:::
:::

     SLIDE 5 — ANOMALY DETECTION
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Anomaly Detection — Spotting the Unusual

An **anomaly** is a data point so far from normal that it deserves attention. We use the simple **3-sigma rule** — flag anything more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

<div class="card card-teal" style="margin-bottom:12px; font-size:0.9em;">
<strong>The Rule</strong><br>
Flag a point if: &nbsp; |value − mean| &nbsp;>&nbsp; 3 × std dev<br>
<span style="font-size:0.85em; color:var(--dgray);">In normal data only 0.3% of days would be flagged. So when the rule fires — something genuinely unusual happened.</span>
</div>

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))

counts = [len(anomalies[anomalies["Period"]==p])
          for p in ["Pre-COVID","COVID Shock","Post-Shock"]]
total  = [len(df[df["Period"]==p])
          for p in ["Pre-COVID","COVID Shock","Post-Shock"]]
pct    = [c/t*100 for c,t in zip(counts,total)]

bars = ax.bar(["Before COVID","COVID Shock","After COVID"],
              pct, color=[TEAL,RED,GREEN], edgecolor="white", width=0.5)
ax.axhline(0.3, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.4, linestyle="--",
           label="Expected in normal data: 0.3%")

for bar, v, c in zip(bars, pct, counts):
    ax.text(bar.get_x()+bar.get_width()/2, v+0.15,
            f"{v:.1f}%\n({c} days)", ha="center",
            fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=bar.get_facecolor())

ax.set_title("% of Days Flagged as Anomaly", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.set_ylabel("% of days"); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
normal_pts = df[~df["Anomaly"]]
ax.plot(normal_pts["Date"], normal_pts["Return"]*100,
        color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.55, label="Normal day")
ax.scatter(anomalies["Date"], anomalies["Return"]*100,
           color=RED, s=55, zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.6,
           label=f"Anomaly ({len(anomalies)} days)")
ax.axhline((mean_r+3*std_r)*100, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.1,
           linestyle=":", alpha=0.8, label="±3σ boundary")
ax.axhline((mean_r-3*std_r)*100, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.1, linestyle=":", alpha=0.8)
ax.axhline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Date"); ax.set_ylabel("Daily Change (%)")
ax.set_title("Anomaly Map — red dots = flagged days", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
⚡ During the shock, **~9% of days were anomalies** — 30× the normal rate. The algorithm found the crisis automatically, using only mean and std dev.
:::
:::
:::

## Summary — 5 Things to Remember

::: {.two-col}

<div class="tk">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tk-n">01</span>
  <span class="tk-t">Time Series = Data in Order</span>
</div>
<div class="tk-b">
A time series is measurements over time — and <strong>order matters.</strong> Monday connects to Tuesday. Shuffle the rows and you destroy the information.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tk">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#0D9488;">
  <span class="tk-n">02</span>
  <span class="tk-t">Trend = Long-Run Direction</span>
</div>
<div class="tk-b">
Smooth out the noise with a <strong>rolling mean</strong> to reveal whether the series is going up, down, or sideways. COVID shows a clear crash then recovery.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tk">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tk-n">03</span>
  <span class="tk-t">Volatility = How Wild It Is</span>
</div>
<div class="tk-b">
Standard deviation of daily changes measures <strong>how much the series jumps around.</strong> COVID pushed volatility 4× above normal — visible instantly in a rolling volatility chart.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tk">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#0D9488;">
  <span class="tk-n">04</span>
  <span class="tk-t">Structural Break = Permanent Change</span>
</div>
<div class="tk-b">
When the series changes behaviour and <strong>stays changed,</strong> that is a structural break. COVID doubled market volatility permanently. Models built on old data fail.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tk">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tk-n">05</span>
  <span class="tk-t">Anomaly Detection = Spot the Unusual</span>
</div>
<div class="tk-b">
The <strong>3-sigma rule</strong> flags anything more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. No labels needed — the data finds its own extreme events automatically.
</div>
</div>

<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0D1B2A,#1A3A5C); border:1px solid var(--teal); border-radius:8px; padding:16px 18px; display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:center;">
  <p style="color:var(--teal2); font-weight:700; font-size:0.82em; letter-spacing:2px; margin:0 0 8px;">THE BIG IDEA</p>
  <p style="color:white; font-size:0.95em; line-height:1.7; margin:0;">
    These tools work on <strong style="color:var(--teal2);">any data over time</strong> — temperature, sales, hospital admissions, energy use. COVID and the stock market are just our learning example.
